summary: J-PAKE is a password-authenticated key exchange protocol. Two parties who share only a password can establish a secure channel over an insecure network without needing a PKI or a trusted third party. This document specifies the protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Two friends who know the same secret word can use it to build a private tunnel, without needing anyone else to vouch for them.

questions: how to do password authenticated key exchange without pki
subtitle: Secure key exchange using only a shared password, without PKI.

tldr.problem: Two parties may need to establish a secure channel using only a password they share, without relying on public key certificates or a trusted third party.
tldr.mechanism: J-PAKE combines Schnorr zero-knowledge proofs with Diffie-Hellman key exchange to prove knowledge of the password and derive a shared session key.
tldr.outcome: Two parties can authenticate each other and exchange keys using passwords alone, with security proofs and resistance to offline dictionary attacks.

today: RFC 8236 is an Informational standard and is not obsoleted. J-PAKE is actively deployed in production systems including Firefox Sync, Google Nest, and Thread IoT networks.

sections.title: What is J-PAKE
sections.content:
J-PAKE stands for Password-Authenticated Key Exchange by Juggling. It is a protocol that lets two parties establish a secure communication channel using only a shared password, with no need for public key certificates or a trusted intermediary.

The protocol was designed by Feng Hao and Peter Ryan in 2008. Unlike earlier password authentication schemes such as EKE (Encrypted Key Exchange), SPEKE, and SRP, J-PAKE has been formally proven secure and resists offline dictionary attacks where an attacker tries to guess the password by analyzing captured network traffic. J-PAKE has seen real-world deployment in products including Firefox sync, Google Nest devices, and the Thread IoT networking standard.
sections.plainLanguage: J-PAKE is a way for two people to prove they know the same password and create an encrypted connection, all without needing a company or server to verify them.

sections.title: How J-PAKE Works
sections.content:
J-PAKE uses two rounds of message exchange. In the first round, each party generates random secret numbers and sends commitments to those numbers along with zero-knowledge proofs that prove they generated the numbers correctly, without revealing the numbers themselves. The other party verifies these proofs.

In the second round, each party uses their private secrets combined with the shared password to compute a value and sends it along with another zero-knowledge proof. Both parties perform the same calculations with their private values and the received commitments, and arrive at the same derived session key. Only parties with the same password can compute the same key. The protocol is symmetric, so both parties play the same role, though it can be adapted to a three-message variant where one party initiates.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two friends writing numbers on paper, putting them in sealed envelopes, and mailing them to each other while also proving they wrote those numbers correctly. Then they use their secret password to transform everything and compute the same final number, which becomes their secret key.

sections.title: Finite Field and Elliptic Curve Variants
sections.content:
J-PAKE can be implemented using either finite field arithmetic (similar to DSA) or elliptic curve arithmetic (similar to ECDSA). In the finite field version, operations are exponentiation modulo a prime; in the elliptic curve version, they are scalar multiplication over an elliptic curve. Both versions provide the same security level and follow the same protocol structure, just with different mathematical operations.

The finite field version requires 14 modular exponentiations total for each party (8 in round one, 4 in round two, and 2 for the final key computation). The elliptic curve version is more efficient, requiring only 11 scalar multiplications total. Both versions must use group parameters providing at least 128-bit security.
sections.plainLanguage: The same protocol can use either the type of math that DSA uses or the type that ECDSA uses. Elliptic curves are faster with the same security level.

sections.title: Security Properties and Key Confirmation
sections.content:
J-PAKE is designed to resist four types of attacks. First, it provides offline dictionary attack resistance: an attacker cannot extract the password from captured messages. Second, it provides forward secrecy: even if the password is later revealed, old session keys remain secure. Third, it offers known-key security: exposure of one session key does not compromise others. Fourth, it limits online dictionary attacks: an active attacker can test only one password per attempt, allowing detection of repeated failed attempts.

After the two rounds complete, both parties have implicitly authenticated each other by deriving the same key. The protocol can optionally include explicit key confirmation, where the parties exchange message authentication codes (MACs) to confirm they both derived the same key. This allows immediate detection of failed authentication attempts and is recommended when network bandwidth permits.
sections.plainLanguage: Even if someone watches all the network traffic, they cannot guess the password offline. Even if the password is later revealed, the old secrets stay secret. And if someone tries many passwords, they get caught quickly.

sections.title: Real-World Use and Status
sections.content: RFC 8236 specifies J-PAKE as an Informational standard. The protocol has been widely adopted in production systems. Mozilla integrated J-PAKE into Firefox Sync and the Network Security Services (NSS) library. Google deployed it in Nest products and has contributed it to open-source libraries. The OpenSSL cryptography library includes a J-PAKE implementation. The protocol has also been adopted by the Thread Alliance as a standard key agreement mechanism for Internet of Things devices and was incorporated into ISO/IEC 11770-4:2017 for key management techniques based on weak secrets.
sections.plainLanguage: Big companies like Mozilla and Google use J-PAKE in products people actually use every day, and it is trusted enough to be in international security standards.
